name: Protein shakes / whey

lead: Whey protein is a powder made from the liquid left over in cheese making, mixed into shakes for convenient protein. Lifters and looksmaxxers use it to support muscle gain and body composition.
A 2010 EFSA panel, as summarised in reference sources, found it roughly as effective as other proteins for muscle and strength.

paras: Whey supplies amino acids that support muscle protein synthesis, especially after resistance exercise.
Whey can trigger milk allergy in some people. It is sold as a food supplement. Studies specific to appearance were not found.

lead: Whey protein is a mixture of proteins isolated from whey, the liquid left when milk is curdled for cheese, and is sold as a powder for protein shakes. It is mainly used to meet protein targets for muscle building and recovery, which looksmaxxing communities link to body composition and a leaner, more muscular frame.[1]

Reference sources report that the European Food Safety Authority in 2010 found no evidence supporting weight-loss claims for whey, and found it about as effective as other protein sources for strength, muscle and lean mass.[1] Human trials listed in registries mostly study appetite, digestion, blood glucose and muscle function in older adults, not facial appearance.

paras: Whey is made by membrane filtration or ion exchange. Concentrate retains some lactose and fat; isolate is typically over 90 percent protein by dry weight; hydrolysate is partially pre-digested and used in hypoallergenic formulas.[1]

In the late 1960s New Zealand's whey surplus prompted research into uses, and in 1970 its dairy research institute produced a 65 percent protein concentrate by ultrafiltration. Coca-Cola launched a whey-fortified drink in Brazil in 1971.[1]

Taking whey after exercise raises circulating amino acids, which supports muscle protein synthesis, according to reference summaries, which also state that pre-exercise intake does not improve performance on its own.[1] Bodybuilding literature lists whey and casein as common supplements, with experts disagreeing on total protein amounts.[2]
Whey proteins are a cause of some milk allergies, though caseins are the major milk allergens.[1]

A randomised crossover trial compared whey, soy and egg white protein on blood glucose after a second meal in normoglycaemic adults.[3] Registered trials have examined whey shakes and appetite or energy intake in people with obesity, and a large program combining exercise and protein supplementation for sarcopenia prevention in older adults.[4][5] No studies were found on whey and facial appearance.
